application_input_paragraph: The petitioner, a member of the Jamaat and person in charge of the Buhari Mosque and Bari Madrasa in Galbokka, Weligama, sought revision of an order dated 15 September 2025 made by the Southern Provincial High Court at Matara in revision application No. 51/2024, which dissolved a stay order previously granted by that High Court staying the execution of a Magistrate's Court order dated 4 April 2024 in case No. 13569. The Magistrate's Court order had been issued under section 15A(3) of the Muslim Mosques and Charitable Trusts or Wakfs Act No. 51 of 1956, directing the Fiscal to deliver possession of the mosque and madrasa property to certain named trustees. The petitioner argued that the trustees had been appointed by the Wakf Board disregarding long‑established custom of appointing trustees from village members, and that proceedings before the Wakf Board and Wakfs Tribunal had been conducted without proper notice or fair hearing. The petitioner contended that the High Court erred in dissolving the stay while appeals were pending before the Wakfs Tribunal and the Court of Appeal. The respondents raised a preliminary jurisdictional objection, arguing that the Court of Appeal could not entertain a revision application against an order made by the Provincial High Court in the exercise of its concurrent revisionary jurisdiction over magistrate's court orders.

The petitioners sought writs of certiorari, mandamus, and prohibition challenging the transfer of one rood of land from permit No. 3673 to the 8th respondent by deed No. 463, registered in the permit register under the Land Development Ordinance. The 1st petitioner held a land grant of two roods under the Land Development Ordinance, and the 2nd petitioner was nominated as successor. The petitioners alleged that the 1st petitioner obtained a loan of Rs. 18,000 from the 7th respondent around 2005, permitted cultivation of a portion until repayment, but the 7th respondent refused repayment, forcibly constructed a building, and colluded with state respondents to obtain a deed transferring one rood to the 8th respondent under duress. Important evidence included the deed P15, register entry P16, the 1st petitioner’s request to cancel the 2nd petitioner’s nomination, the Divisional Secretary’s consent letters (1R13-1R17), and a 1999 agreement X1 signed by the 1st petitioner. The main grounds of appeal were that the respondents failed to follow the Land Development Ordinance procedure, particularly section 162(2), and that the deed registered in the permit register was null and void. The respondents contended that the petitioners were guilty of laches, misrepresented material facts, failed to come with clean hands, did not name necessary parties, and the application was frivolous. The defence position (of the 7th and 8th respondents) was that the loan and transfer occurred in 1999, the 1st petitioner voluntarily transferred the land for Rs. 18,000, and the respondents had possessed and cultivated the land since 1999.

The petitioner, a Leading Infantry in the Sri Lanka Navy with over 16 years of service, was summarily tried on three charges of disciplinary offences under section 104(1) of the Navy Act: illegally bringing cigarettes into camp and selling them at exorbitant rates to recruits; surreptitiously bringing cannabis, a prohibited substance, into camp and selling it to recruits; and making and smoking cannabis cigarettes. The Summary Trial was conducted by the 2nd Respondent on 02.03.2021, resulting in a conviction on all charges and a punishment of dismissal without disgrace from the Navy. The case arose after the petitioner reported an officer for assaulting a recruit, following which he was taken into custody by the Naval Provost Branch, allegedly assaulted, and coerced into making incriminating statements. A key witness, Recruit Chandrasiri, later stated his statement implicating the petitioner was made under duress. The petitioner challenged the trial on multiple grounds, including failure to serve a charge sheet, denial of a defending officer of his choice, incorrect recording of a guilty plea, denial of the opportunity to cross-examine the sole prosecution witness or call defence witnesses, failure to adduce reasons for the verdict, and the imposition of an excessive and ultra vires punishment. The respondents maintained that the petitioner, as a junior sailor, was only entitled to a Summary Trial, that he pleaded guilty validly, and that the procedure was properly followed.

The accused-appellant was indicted under the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance for possession and trafficking of 21.44 grams of heroin. The High Court of Balapitiya convicted him on both counts and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The case arose from a police raid on 13 January 2013, during which a parcel of heroin was allegedly recovered from the appellant. Important evidence included the prosecution's failure to record odometer readings, lack of sealing equipment at the raid, discrepancies in the location of the raid, a damaged cover that led to the Government Analyst Department initially refusing to accept the productions, and serious lapses in the chain of custody, including a 12.33 gram weight discrepancy and a police officer retaining the productions in his personal locker for two days. The main grounds of appeal were that the learned High Court Judge failed to consider the prosecution evidence untrustworthy when tested by the standard of probability and failed to properly evaluate the evidence of a police officer regarding the refusal and resealing of the productions. The defence position was that the prosecution evidence, particularly the chain of custody, was unreliable and compromised, rendering the conviction unsafe.

The petitioner was indicted in the High Court of Colombo on charges of having committed offences under Sections 328, 329 and 298 of the Penal Code arising out of a motor traffic accident, and the learned High Court Judge convicted the petitioner on counts 01, 02, 04 and 09, sentencing him to fines and imprisonment including 5 years rigorous imprisonment on count 01 and count 02, 2 years rigorous imprisonment on count 09, and various default sentences and compensation orders, while acquitting him on other counts. Aggrieved by the conviction and sentence, the petitioner preferred an appeal to the Court of Appeal on 14 December 2023. The petitioner then applied for bail pending appeal in the High Court, which was refused on 22 May 2024. In support of his revision application against that refusal, the petitioner contended that the learned High Court Judge erred in law by disguising the judgment in Dachchaini v The Attorney General, by refusing bail on the basis that there were no exceptional circumstances, by failing to apply the criteria set out in Dachchaini, and by failing to consider the medical condition of the petitioner's wife, the nature of the offence, and that it would be unlikely that the petitioner would abscond. The defence position argued that the exceptional circumstances test is not found in the Criminal Procedure Act or the Bail Act, and that a test similar to Section 14(1) of the Bail Act should be adopted for bail pending appeal.

The appellant, Athige Rohitha Kusumsiri, as a director of Eco Uniware (Pvt) Ltd, faced proceedings under Section 38(2) of the Employees' Provident Fund Act No. 15 of 1958 before the Magistrate's Court of Galgamuwa for recovery of unpaid EPF contributions and surcharge amounting to Rs. 1,883,648. The Magistrate ordered that the sum be recovered from the appellant personally as a fine, with a default sentence of six months imprisonment with light work, relying on Section 40 of the EPF Act to impose personal liability on the director. The High Court of Kurunegala dismissed a revision application, affirming the Magistrate's order. On appeal, the main ground was that Section 40 only applies in criminal prosecutions for offences under the Act and cannot be invoked in recovery proceedings under Section 38(2), which are not criminal in nature. The defence position was that the appellant's appearance before the court was purely procedural as a representative of the company and did not create personal liability, and that the Magistrate exceeded jurisdiction by treating the recovery proceeding as a means to impose criminal liability on a director.

The accused-appellant was indicted for the murder of Peramuna Arachchige Somasiri on 24/02/2012, an offence punishable under Section 296 of the Penal Code. The High Court of Embilipitiya found the appellant guilty and sentenced him to death on 09/11/2023. The prosecution case was that the appellant had a long-standing dispute with the deceased, his father-in-law, and on the day of the incident threatened the deceased and his wife at a bank premises, later deliberately colliding his van with the deceased's three-wheeler, causing death. The defence maintained that the collision was purely accidental, caused by avoiding a recklessly overtaking truck, and that the appellant did not know the deceased would be travelling that route; he helped admit the deceased to hospital and remained at the scene. The sole ground of appeal was that the totality of evidence did not support a murderous intention beyond reasonable doubt but rather pointed to lesser culpability on the basis of knowledge or a mitigatory plea.

The accused-appellant was charged under Section 296 of the Penal Code for the murder of Majeed Anzar on 24.04.2009. The High Court of Matale convicted him and imposed the death sentence. The prosecution case was that the appellant chased and fatally stabbed the deceased with a knife. No eyewitness directly observed the infliction of fatal injuries, but witnesses saw the appellant chasing the deceased and later holding a knife, and a police officer saw the bleeding victim being pursued by a man with a knife. The Judicial Medical Officer recorded eleven injuries and opined the knife was compatible. The appellant claimed he acted in the exercise of the right of private defence, asserting that the deceased, a person of notorious character involved in illegal drugs and illicit liquor, had previously inflicted grievous injury on him, uttered threatening words shortly before the incident, and advanced toward him, causing sudden fear. A defence witness testified the deceased habitually carried a knife. The grounds of appeal were that the prosecution failed to prove the appellant caused the death and that the trial judge failed to consider mitigating circumstances amounting to private defence.

The Appellant was indicted under Section 365 B(2)(b) of the Penal Code for two counts of grave sexual abuse of a nine-year-old girl. The High Court of Tangalle convicted him on both counts and sentenced him to eight years rigorous imprisonment per count, a fine of Rs.5,000 per count with a default sentence of three months rigorous imprisonment, and compensation of Rs.300,000 with a default sentence of six months simple imprisonment, the custodial sentences to run concurrently. The brief facts are that the Appellant, a neighbour, took the victim to a room adjacent to her kitchen and committed intercrural sex, and the victim's mother witnessed the act and lodged a police complaint the same day. Important evidence included the victim's vivid testimony, the mother's prompt complaint, and a police statement recorded on 21 September 2011 admitted under Section 420 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The main grounds of appeal were that the prosecution failed to prove the specific date of the second count beyond reasonable doubt and framed an invalid charge for the first count, that the probability of the incident was doubtful, and that the learned High Court Judge failed to analyse the evidence beyond reasonable doubt. The defence position was that based on the evidence offered, it was impossible to conclude that the prosecution had proven its case beyond reasonable doubt.

The appellant was indicted in the High Court of Kurunegala for the murder of Rajamuni Dewayalage Pini on or about 24 December 1995, punishable under Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code. The High Court convicted the appellant and sentenced him to death, while acquitting the second accused. The prosecution case was that the appellant and another arrived on a motorcycle at the deceased’s shop, and the appellant stabbed the deceased with a knife, causing fatal injuries. The sole eyewitness, a seven-year-old granddaughter of the deceased, initially identified the assailants by name as Jayasuriya and Sunil, but later contradicted herself by claiming she did not know their names. She identified only the appellant at the identification parade and failed to identify the second accused, despite stating they were known to her. The defence challenged the identification, highlighted material contradictions and omissions, and argued that the witness’s credibility was undermined. The appellant made a dock statement. Grounds of appeal included errors in failing to act under Section 196 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, failure to consider contradictions in identification evidence, failure to apply the test of probability, and failure to properly assess the credibility of the sole eyewitness.

The Accused-Appellant, a Grama Niladhari, was convicted in the High Court of Colombo on four counts of soliciting and accepting a bribe from a disabled person, Abhabinna Arachchige Anura Bandara Abesinghe, punishable under Section 19(b) and (c) of the Bribery Act. The High Court sentenced him to five years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 5,000 for each count, with one year rigorous imprisonment in default for each count, a further fine of Rs. 25,000 with one year in default, and for the fourth count ordered compensation of Rs. 100,000 to the victim with two years in default. The case arose when the Appellant, while informing PW 01 about a government housing donation for disabled persons, solicited Rs. 25,000 from each of the four instalments, totalling Rs. 100,000. A trap was laid by the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption, during which PW 01 handed over the demanded money and the Appellant instructed him to place it under a bag on the table; a letter bearing the Appellant’s seal was also recovered. The decoy (PW 03) witnessed the transaction and the raid party recovered the money. The main grounds of appeal challenged the credibility of the decoy, the sufficiency of evidence on the charges, the failure to properly evaluate the defence evidence, and the legality of the compensation order. The defence contended that a personal dispute motivated a false complaint, that the money was planted among documents, and that discrepancies between PW 01 and PW 03 weakened the prosecution case. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding the prosecution had proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and affirming the conviction and sentence.

The accused-appellant was indicted on three counts of grave sexual abuse of a minor under Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code. The High Court convicted him on the first count, sentencing him to 12 years of rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 10,000 with a default sentence of 10 months rigorous imprisonment, and ordered compensation of Rs. 100,000 to the victim, while acquitting him on the second and third counts. The victim, the appellant's daughter, testified that in 2013 and 2014, when she was 10 years old and her mother was on night shift, the appellant removed her clothing and inserted his male organ into her vagina on multiple occasions, threatening to kill her mother. She disclosed the abuse to a neighbour and later at a school seminar attended by police. The appellant gave a dock statement denying the allegations and claimed the victim's mother had instructed the child to falsely accuse him due to the mother's alleged extramarital affair. The prosecution led evidence from six witnesses and produced two documents. The main grounds of appeal were that the trial judge misdirected himself by failing to consider the uncertainty surrounding the first information, failing to consider the presumption under section 114(t) of the Evidence Ordinance due to suppression of material witnesses, omitting to evaluate the absence of conclusive medical corroboration, failing to consider the impact of family conflict and institutional care on the child's credibility, failing to appreciate the need for corroboration of the child's testimony, rejecting the dock statement solely for lack of prior cross-examination without assessing its independent probative value, failing to consider a plausible alternative explanation referred to as the ghost factor, and failing to consider the appellant's socio-economic condition as a mitigating factor in sentencing.

The accused-appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possession of 11.10 grams of heroin under Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance and sentenced to life imprisonment on both counts. The prosecution case was that on 27 August 2013, acting on information from Police Constable Dinesh, a police team arrested the appellant near a ‘watta’ by Sumithrarama temple and recovered a parcel of heroin from his pocket; the informant and PC Dinesh were not called as witnesses. The appellant’s defence was that he was arrested at his residence, not at the scene, and was implicated solely because he had telephoned the other arrested person. Important evidence included contradictory testimony from the two main police witnesses regarding the place of arrest and the existence of a three-way junction, as well as the failure to call PC Dinesh, which created a vital missing link. The main grounds of appeal were that the prosecution witnesses lacked credibility due to material contradictions and that the trial judge had rejected the defence evidence on unreasonable grounds while wrongly reversing the burden of proof onto the appellant to prove his innocence.

The matter arose from an application filed by the Competent Authority, Sri Lanka Ports Authority, under section 5 of the State Lands (Recovery of Possession) Act No. 7 of 1979 in the Magistrate's Court of Galle for the eviction of the respondent-petitioner-petitioner from a land described as State land. The learned Additional Magistrate rejected the preliminary objections that the land was not State land but belonged to the Forest Conservation Department and that the applicant was not a validly appointed competent authority, and ordered eviction. The High Court dismissed the revision application. The petitioner then sought revision from the Court of Appeal, contending that the land was not State land vested in the Ports Authority and that the competent authority had not submitted the minister’s written approval or the instrument of appointment with the application, thus the eviction order was unlawful. The defence position was that the land belonged to the Forest Conservation Department and the competent authority lacked lawful authority. The Court of Appeal examined the statutory scheme, including sections 3(1), 5(1), 9(1) and 9(2) of the Act, and held that the occupant is precluded from contesting the competent authority’s opinion that the land is State land, the only permissible defence being possession under a valid permit or written authority of the State, which was not established; further, under the decision in Wedamulla v. Abeysinghe, the production of the minister’s approval and appointment document was not a condition precedent, and the presumption of regularity applied.

The appellant filed an information under section 66(1)(b) of the Primary Courts Procedure Act in the Magistrate’s Court alleging that the respondents had forcibly dispossessed him from a portion of a building on 3 February 2010. The land and building were co-owned by multiple parties, including the appellant and the first respondent. The Magistrate, after inquiry, found that the appellant had not proved possession of the entire premises and that the respondents had established possession of the disputed portion, and made an order under section 68(3) prohibiting the appellant from disturbing the respondents’ possession. The appellant applied to the High Court in revision to set aside that order, but the High Court dismissed the application, holding that no exceptional circumstances existed to warrant revision because an alternative remedy—a partition action—was already pending in the District Court and the Magistrate’s order was not palpably wrong. The main grounds of appeal before the Court of Appeal were that the High Court erred in declining to exercise revisionary jurisdiction and in failing to correct the Magistrate’s alleged errors. The defence maintained that the respondents were co-owners in continuous possession and that the appellant had not been dispossessed. Key evidence included document X6 recording that possession of the building had been handed over to nine persons, deeds of gift and transfer, and the pending partition actions.

The appellant was indicted for murder under section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code along with two others. After a non-jury trial, the High Court convicted him and imposed the death sentence. The case concerned the death of Meegaha Kankanamge Dhanuka Rathnasiri. PW1, a cousin of the deceased, heard distressed cries and later found the injured deceased. The sole eyewitness, PW2, testified that she saw only two individuals at the scene—one holding the deceased’s legs and the other kneeling beside him—and could identify only one of them; she did not state that the appellant attacked the deceased. The main grounds of appeal included misdirections in the trial judge’s evaluation of PW2’s evidence, such as concluding that three accused assaulted the deceased with sharp weapons and that PW2 heard the deceased plead not to be assaulted, contrary to the evidence; summarily rejecting the appellant’s alibi solely for want of prior notice without considering it on its merits; drawing an adverse inference from an alleged six-month evasion of arrest unsupported by evidence; and making unwarranted speculative remarks. The defence maintained that the appellant’s identification was not proven beyond reasonable doubt and that the alibi raised a reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal held that the trial judge’s findings were based on conjecture, rendering the conviction unsafe, and consequently allowed the appeal and acquitted the appellant.

The accused-appellant was convicted in the High Court of Tangalle on two counts of grave sexual abuse contrary to section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code, having initially pleaded not guilty and then changed his plea to guilty after five prosecution witnesses had testified. He was sentenced to ten years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 5,000 (default three months' rigorous imprisonment) on the first count, twelve years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 5,000 (default three months' rigorous imprisonment) on the second count, and ordered to pay Rs. 400,000 as compensation (default six months' simple imprisonment), with all sentences to run consecutively. The victim was a 16-year-old boy who was alone at an isolated spot; the 22-year-old appellant assaulted him, forced him to remove his clothes, inserted his penis into the victim's anus, compelled the victim to perform oral sex, took Rs. 2,500 from the victim's purse, and threatened to hand him over to the police while falsely claiming to be a police officer. The Medico-Legal Report documented anal tears, fresh bleeding, and a traumatic perforation of the eardrum. The sole ground of appeal was that the sentence imposed was excessive. The defence submitted only the appellant's young age as a mitigating factor and did not advance any other mitigation.

The case concerns a dispute affecting land likely to cause a breach of the peace, initiated by the police filing information under section 66(1)(a) of the Primary Courts Procedure Act No. 44 of 1979 before the Magistrate Court of Marawila. The Appellants (first party) alleged they were lawful owners in possession and had been unlawfully and forcefully dispossessed by the Respondents (second party) on 25 March 2007. The Respondents denied the allegation and claimed lawful ownership and possession. The Magistrate, after inquiry, found that the Appellants had not established possession at the time of filing the information on 4 April 2007 or that they had been forcefully dispossessed, and determined that the Respondents were in possession; the Appellants were ordered to file a civil suit to resolve their rights. The Appellants sought revision in the High Court of Chilaw, which dismissed the revision application on 26 March 2021. The main grounds of appeal before the Court of Appeal were that the High Court erred in not exercising revisionary jurisdiction to set aside the Magistrate’s order. The defence position was that the Magistrate’s order was correct and that the Appellants had an alternative remedy by way of civil suit. Important evidence included the Appellant’s complaint to police on 30 March 2007, which complained only of forceful plucking of coconuts and did not allege forceful dispossession, supporting the finding that no dispossession was established. No conviction or sentence was imposed as the matter involved a possession determination under Part VII of the Act.

The appellant was charged in the High Court of Colombo with possession of 3.58 grams of heroin under Section 54A(d) and trafficking the same quantity under Section 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance. The High Court convicted the appellant on both counts and sentenced her to life imprisonment. The prosecution case was that on 27 September 2021, police officers raided the appellant's residence at Samithipura, Mattakkuliya, where a female officer recovered a heroin parcel from the appellant's frock pocket. Key evidence included the testimonies of the searching officer (PW7) and the lead investigator (PW1), which contained contradictions about where the police vehicle stopped, PW7's failure to make contemporaneous notes of the weighing and sealing, and her certification of PW1's notes without observing those steps. It was also elicited that PW1 had arrested a relative of the appellant at a different address. The main grounds of appeal were that the trial judge failed to properly assess the credibility of contradictory and improbable prosecution evidence, gave inadequate consideration to procedural lapses that compromised the chain of custody, and failed to properly evaluate the defence. In her dock statement, the appellant asserted that the police had come in search of her husband, that she was instructed to call him without revealing the police presence, and that she was arrested immediately after informing him, creating a reasonable doubt as to the prosecution's version.

The appellant was indicted in the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 10.28 grams of heroin, offences under section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance. The High Court convicted him on both counts and sentenced him to death. The prosecution case was that on 16 June 2016, police officers on routine duty arrested the appellant near Andrewge Watta, Mahawaththa, and found a parcel of heroin in his possession. Important evidence included the testimonies of PW1 and PW2, who gave contradictory accounts of which officers participated in the search and arrest, and PW2’s failure to record significant matters despite acknowledging their importance; the police did not search the appellant’s residence, which was located 50–70 metres away. The appellant made a dock statement asserting that he was arrested at his home, not near the Buddha statue as alleged. The main grounds of appeal were that the trial judge failed to consider the inter se discrepancies in the evidence of PW1 and PW2, erroneously evaluated the defence evidence by placing it in juxtaposition with the prosecution case and predetermining guilt, and misdirected himself by imposing a burden on the appellant to prove his dock statement through witnesses. The defence maintained that the dock statement created a reasonable doubt about the place of arrest.

The accused-appellant was indicted with two others for the murder of Godawatthage Lalith Susantha under Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code. The High Court convicted the appellant and sentenced him to death while acquitting the co-accused. The prosecution case relied on the sole eyewitness PW1, the mother of the deceased, who testified that in 2001 she saw the appellant shoot the deceased at Pattanbugodawatta as the deceased was with a friend; she lodged a prompt complaint. Medical evidence confirmed firearm injuries, and the Government Analyst’s report concerned cartridges recovered from the scene, while the pistol marked P3 was not conclusively identified by PW1. The defence marked eight contradictions (D1–D8) in PW1’s evidence, covering peripheral matters such as her exact position and the number of shots fired. The main grounds of appeal were that the judgment violated Section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, the trial judge improperly assessed PW1’s credibility, the Government Analyst’s report created a reasonable doubt, PW1’s testimony contained material contradictions and was inconsistent with medical and ballistic evidence, and the trial judge failed to record compliance with Section 200(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act regarding the defence. The defence maintained that the sole eyewitness was unreliable, the prosecution failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt, and procedural omissions prejudiced the appellant.

The accused-appellants were convicted by the High Court of Kalutara on five counts: being a member of an unlawful assembly under section 140 of the Penal Code, committing murder under section 296 read with section 140, committing grievous hurt under section 317 read with section 140, and the substantive offences of murder under section 296 and grievous hurt under section 317. The High Court sentenced the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 5th accused to death for murder, two years rigorous imprisonment for the unlawful assembly and grievous hurt counts, and ordered compensation. The prosecution case was that on 02.01.1996, following a dispute over shrimp trading, the 1st accused struck the deceased on the head with a manna knife and the other accused joined in attacking the deceased and PW1, causing the deceased’s death in hospital. Eyewitnesses PW1 and PW2 gave consistent accounts that the 1st accused used a manna knife, and the Judicial Medical Officer stated the fatal blunt-force head injury could have been caused by the blunt side of such a knife. The main ground of appeal was a material contradiction between the eyewitness description of a knife and the medical evidence of a blunt weapon. The defence denied involvement, raised alibis, and challenged witness credibility. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, affirming the convictions and sentences.

The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Chilaw on three counts of rape of a minor under 16 years, contrary to section 364(2) of the Penal Code (Amendment) Act No.22 of 1995, and sentenced to 18 years rigorous imprisonment on each count to run concurrently, with fines of Rs.5000 each and an order to pay Rs.800,000 compensation to the victim. The complainant was a 15-year-old girl whom the appellant, then a 27-year-old married man acting as her de facto guardian, raped on multiple occasions between November 2006 and April 2007. DNA evidence confirmed that the appellant was the father of the child born to the complainant. The appellant pleaded guilty only at the tail end of the trial and advanced mitigation including his age, absence of prior convictions, family circumstances, and the plea of guilt. The sole ground of appeal was that the sentence of 18 years rigorous imprisonment was disproportionate and excessive. The Court of Appeal found the sentence proportionate in light of the aggravating circumstances, dismissed the appeal, and affirmed the conviction and sentence.

The appellant was convicted in the High Court of Ratnapura on the first count under section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code and sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs.10,000 with a default sentence of 3 months rigorous imprisonment, and compensation of Rs.150,000 with a default sentence of 6 months rigorous imprisonment; he was acquitted on the second and third counts. The complainant was a 14-year-old schoolgirl who went to the appellant's house seeking his wife; the appellant dragged her to the kitchen, removed her clothes, and performed intercrual sex, having told her not to shout. Later that evening he held her hand, and on a previous occasion he had held her from behind in a vegetable garden. The incident was disclosed to the appellant's wife and then to the victim's father, leading to a police complaint. The Judicial Medical Officer did not exclude sexual abuse but ruled out rape. A police officer recorded a second statement from the victim on 03.03.2015 on the direction of the Attorney General because of perceived contradictions in the first statement, but the prosecution failed to tender that statement to the defence or the court. The appellant gave evidence denying the charges and called his wife as a witness. The main grounds of appeal were that the non-disclosure of the second statement violated the right to a fair trial under Article 13(3) of the Constitution and caused grave prejudice, and that the appellant had already been indicted and convicted in a separate case (HCR/38/2017) on the same incident after pleading guilty to a reduced charge of sexual harassment based on the same Medico-Legal Report, rendering the present prosecution improper.

The accused-appellant was indicted in the High Court of Kaluthara for the murder of Dayawathi Kaluarrachchi, his mother, under section 296 of the Penal Code, and for robbery of a gold ring under section 380. The High Court convicted him of murder and sentenced him to death, while acquitting him of robbery. The deceased, who lived with the appellant, had previously confided in her niece (PW01) that she was being harassed and feared for her life. On the day in question, PW01 found the deceased injured on the kitchen floor; the deceased stated “Kelum hit me”, identifying her son. She was hospitalised and later died. The post‑mortem examination documented five head and face injuries and right‑side brain bleeding, with intracerebral haemorrhage from blunt trauma as the cause of death. Medical evidence indicated she retained the ability to speak when found and that the absence of limb or hip injuries made a fall unlikely. The appellant’s defence was that he had gone to town to pawn a ring and buy medicine and was not present at the time, returning to find the deceased already taken to hospital. The main grounds of appeal were that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt on circumstantial evidence, that the dying declaration was not considered in its correct perspective, and that the trial judge failed to consider the defence case.

The accused-appellants were convicted by the High Court of Gampaha for the murder of Samantha Kumara under Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that on 1 August 2017, the appellants, armed with an iron pipe and a Manna knife, entered the deceased’s house, broke windows, and attacked him, causing fatal injuries. The wife and 12-year-old son of the deceased testified as eyewitnesses to the assault. The defence contended that the deceased owed money to the appellants, that he attacked them first with a rod and a knife, and that they acted in private defence after the wife threw chilli water. The grounds of appeal alleged failure to properly evaluate contradictory eyewitness testimony, improper admission of evidence under section 27(1) of the Evidence Ordinance, erroneous analysis of private defence and sudden fight, incorrect finding of common intention, and failure to prove murder beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal found the discrepancies between the witnesses immaterial and concluded that the trial judge correctly rejected the plea of private defence, noting that the appellants sustained no injuries while the deceased suffered multiple wounds, and upheld the conviction.

The accused-appellants were convicted by the High Court under sections 140 (unlawful assembly), 296 read with 146 (murder), and 314 read with 146 (simple hurt) of the Penal Code, and sentenced to death for murder along with terms of imprisonment and fines for the other counts. The prosecution case was that on 20 June 2004, following a dispute over three-wheeler hires, the appellants and another attacked the deceased and his brother (PW1) with knives and clubs, causing injuries that led to the deceased's death from haemorrhagic shock due to multiple cut wounds. The key evidence was the eyewitness testimony of the deceased’s brother, who identified all the assailants, supported by medical evidence of eight cut injuries and a purported dying declaration. On appeal, the appellants argued that the trial judge failed to properly evaluate the dying declaration and conflicts between the eyewitness account, the medical evidence, and the investigation officer’s testimony; that the sole eyewitness was unreliable due to contradictions, omissions, and improbability; that the rejection of the alibi under section 126A of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act was a misdirection; that the identification of certain appellants was doubtful; and that the judgment was deficient and shifted the burden of proof. The Court of Appeal, after reviewing the evidence and the trial judge’s analysis, dismissed all grounds of appeal, holding that the prosecution had proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and affirming the convictions and sentences.

The appellant was indicted in the High Court of Gampaha for grave sexual abuse of an 11-year-old boy, alleged to have occurred on 19 September 2015, involving oral sexual acts in a three-wheeler and showing pornographic material. The High Court convicted the appellant and imposed a sentence of 8 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 150,000 with a default term of 1 year simple imprisonment, and compensation of Rs. 20,000 to the victim. The prosecution relied on the evidence of the child victim, his mother to whom a prompt complaint was made, and the medical officer who examined the victim five days later and recorded a history of multiple prior sexual acts, though no physical injuries were found. The defence denied the allegation, suggesting the victim had behavioural issues, had previously made a similar complaint against another person, and that on the day in question the victim had grabbed the appellant’s organ causing his prosthetic leg to detach. The main grounds of appeal were that the trial judge failed to properly evaluate material inconsistencies between the testimony of the victim, his mother, and the medical officer, particularly the omission from the victim’s trial evidence of earlier incidents that he had recounted to the doctor, and that the prosecution had not proved the case beyond a reasonable doubt.

The appellant was indicted for committing rape on a female under the age of 16, an offence punishable under section 364(2)e of the Penal Code. The High Court convicted him and imposed a sentence of 18 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 10,000 with a default sentence of 12 months simple imprisonment, and compensation of Rs. 750,000 with a default sentence of 24 months simple imprisonment. The victim, a schoolgirl below 16, was at home with her sleeping grandmother when the appellant entered, asked for water, then grabbed her from behind, threatened her with a knife, and raped her. She later reported the incident to her parents and was taken to hospital, where she underwent surgery. Unchallenged evidence established that after the rape he ensured she was bleeding and that she had not reached puberty. On appeal, learned counsel confined submissions to the sentence, arguing it was excessive in light of the minimum mandatory sentence of 10 years, and urged that the appellant—aged 36, married, a father of one child, the sole breadwinner, and now repentant—deserved clemency because of the hardship his incarceration would cause his family.

The petitioner, an entrepreneur who invested in a condominium complex named 'Sanasa Purahala' in Naiwala, Weyangoda, filed an application for writs of certiorari, prohibition, and mandamus against police officers, seeking to compel them to remove unauthorized three-wheeler parking and to prosecute the drivers for public nuisance. The underlying criminal case in the Magistrate's Court of Attanagalla (No. B/2406/22) involved 19 three-wheeler drivers charged by police with criminal trespass and unlawful restraint under Sections 433 and 332 of the Penal Code, but the Magistrate refused to add a charge of public nuisance after finding no prima facie case, noting that some occupants of the complex did not view the parking as a nuisance and no exact demarcation of the parking area was established. The petitioner contended that the police had a duty under Section 73 of the Police Ordinance and Section 170 of the Municipal Councils Ordinance to take action on the basis of public nuisance, and relied on photographic evidence, survey plans, and correspondence with local authorities to show the hindrance. The respondent police officers argued that the pending criminal trespass case precluded the writ, that the alleged perpetrators and the Municipal Council were not made parties, and that no public element for nuisance had been established.

The appellant was indicted before the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 3.5 grams of Heroin. The High Court convicted him and imposed a sentence of life imprisonment. The prosecution case was that police officers on patrol received information that the appellant was proceeding to deliver heroin; they intercepted him, recovered a parcel of heroin concealed under his sarong, later weighed the substance at a pawn shop, and sent the productions to the Government Analyst. The defence gave a dock statement and called two witnesses asserting that the appellant was arrested at his residence, not on the road as alleged. On appeal, the main grounds were that the trial judge failed to consider infirmities such as the lack of odometer readings, the unexplained decision to use an external scale despite carrying one, the absence of contemporaneous notes, the failure to search other occupants at the appellant's residence, and a significant gap in the chain of custody of the productions between 08.02.2017 and 21.03.2017, as well as the erroneous approach of evaluating prosecution evidence in isolation before considering the defence, thereby reversing the presumption of innocence.

The Accused-Appellant was indicted in the High Court of Balapitiya on one count of abduction under Section 354 of the Penal Code and two counts of rape under Section 364(2)(e), committed against a 14-year-old girl. He pleaded guilty on all counts and was sentenced to one year rigorous imprisonment and a fine for abduction, ten years rigorous imprisonment and a fine for each rape count (to run concurrently), and ordered to pay Rs. 200,000 compensation. The victim stated that she had a romantic relationship with the appellant but did not consent to sexual activities; she was 14 and the appellant 28 at the time of the offences. The appellant abandoned his appeal against conviction and pursued only an appeal against sentence, pleading in mitigation that he had no previous convictions, had pleaded guilty, and that the parties were in a consensual romantic relationship, while also invoking Supreme Court precedent for leniency in imposing a sentence below the statutory minimum. The prosecution highlighted the victim’s lack of consent and her young age as aggravating factors. The Court of Appeal found that the High Court judge had carefully balanced the aggravating and mitigating circumstances, imposed a sentence within the prescribed range, and that no interference was warranted.

The accused-appellants were indicted in the High Court of Kalutara for the murder of Prematilaka Hettiarachchi on 6 March 1998, charged under sections 140, 146 and 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code; following a non-jury trial, the first, second, third and fourth appellants were acquitted on two counts but convicted on the third count of murder and sentenced to death on 11 June 2020. The prosecution case rested primarily on the sole eyewitness, PW1 (the deceased’s nephew), who testified that he and the deceased were ambushed near a bridge while on a motorcycle; the first appellant struck the deceased’s head with a manna knife, and the second and fourth appellants, armed with iron rods, attacked the deceased and threw stones at PW1. Medical evidence recorded nine injuries, with death caused by cranio-cerebral injuries from cut injuries to the head. The defence consisted of unsworn dock statements by the second appellant and the fifth accused (who was acquitted), which the trial judge rejected, while the remaining appellants remained silent. On appeal, the convicted appellants argued that the trial judge misdirected himself by convicting on the uncorroborated testimony of a discredited single witness, failed to address material contradictions and omissions, and did not properly evaluate key witness evidence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and affirmed the conviction and death sentence.

The petitioner, along with three others, was indicted under the Bribery Act by the Director General of the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption. Following a full trial, the High Court of Colombo convicted all four accused and imposed a jail sentence and a fine. The petitioner filed a statutory appeal against the High Court judgment, and while that appeal remained pending, he invoked the revisionary jurisdiction of the Court of Appeal. He raised grounds that the High Court judge overstepped judicial boundaries, committed grave procedural improprieties denying a fair hearing, arbitrarily disregarded material and exculpatory evidence, violated the presumption of innocence, and misapplied legal principles including the burden of proof and the Ellenborough dictum; he further alleged that the indictment was defective, the prosecution impermissibly shifted its position, and the investigation was tainted.

The accused-appellant, a Grama Seva Officer, was charged before the High Court of Colombo with soliciting and accepting a bribe of Rs.6000 from Punchihewa Rasika Lakmal in October 2013 for assisting in preparing and issuing land permits, offences punishable under sections 19(a), 19(c), 19(a) and 19(d) of the Bribery Act. The High Court convicted him on all four charges and imposed concurrent sentences of three years rigorous imprisonment per charge, fines of Rs.5000 each with default terms, and an additional fine of Rs.6000 under section 26 of the Act. The prosecution case was that the appellant solicited and accepted the money from the virtual complainant (PW1), who sought a permit for state-owned land occupied by his uncle; a trap was arranged by the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption, leading to the appellant’s arrest on 04 November 2013 with the tainted money. Key evidence included testimony from PW1, the decoy (PW2) and the raiding officer (PW3), with discrepancies regarding the date of the raid and the exact location of the arrest—whether inside the office or in the corridor. The appellant’s defence was that he was falsely implicated due to a misrepresented introduction and that any payment discussed related to surveying a different land, but this was not put to prosecution witnesses. The main grounds of appeal were that the trial judge failed to consider inconsistencies, applied wrong criteria in evaluating evidence, and rejected the defence on a wrong premise. The Court of Appeal, taking a holistic view and relying on the appellant’s own dock statement to clarify the raid date, found the discrepancies immaterial, noted the complaint was prompt, and held that the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

The appellants were charged in the High Court of Kalutara with being members of an unlawful assembly with the common object of injuring Udugepalage Rafiel, committing his murder as members of an unlawful assembly, and murder based on common intention. The High Court convicted the appellants on all charges and imposed the death sentence. The prosecution case relied on the testimony of a sole eyewitness, PW01, who claimed he saw the appellants and the first accused attack the deceased with bill hook knives and clubs while he hid in a tea plantation. The post-mortem report recorded eight cut injuries and two contusions, with death due to hemorrhagic shock. The defence denied involvement, and the fourth accused raised an alibi. On appeal, the appellants argued that PW01’s evidence was unreliable because of material contradictions with his police statement, an unexplained seven-day delay in making that statement, and the physical improbability of his claimed observations from his hiding place. They also contended that the trial judge misdirected himself on the alibi, failed to properly assess the challenge to PW01’s credibility, and omitted the required legal analysis of unlawful assembly and common intention. The Court of Appeal set aside the convictions and death sentence and acquitted the appellants.

The appellant was indicted before the High Court of Colombo on two counts of grave sexual abuse under Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code and one count of sexual harassment under Section 345, allegedly committed against Tashmila Didulani Rukshan, a minor aged 13 years and 8 months, between 12 August 2013 and 11 August 2014. The High Court convicted him as charged and sentenced him to 10 years rigorous imprisonment and a Rs 20,000 fine on each grave sexual abuse count, and 2 years rigorous imprisonment and a Rs 10,000 fine on the sexual harassment count, with default sentences and all terms to run concurrently. The case facts were that the appellant, a close relative by marriage, touched the victim’s chest underneath her T‑shirt while she watched television, touched her genital area over her clothes and kissed her ear while she was in bed, and on another occasion hugged her from behind when she was leaving a room after washing; the victim did not complain until a financial dispute arose between the families, after which she told her mother and a police complaint was lodged. The prosecution led the victim’s testimony, which lacked precise dates, and the evidence of a JMO who found no external injuries but referred her for psychiatric assessment due to sadness. The main grounds of appeal were the non‑consideration of the delay in complaint and its impact on a fair trial, the failure to legally analyse the belated complaint, the erroneous application of the ingredients of grave sexual abuse and the burden of proof, and the failure to evaluate unchallenged defence evidence. The defence position was that the acts were mere touching falling short of grave sexual abuse, the complaint was belated, and the familial relationship explained continued visits, and the appellant denied the charges, gave evidence and called witnesses.

The appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo of murder under section 296 of the Penal Code for causing the death of Samraj Sankar Raj and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that on 1 January 2010 at Fort, Colombo, following a verbal altercation between the deceased and the second accused, the fourth accused restrained the deceased, the second accused inflicted a knife wound to the abdomen, and the appellant then struck the deceased on the head with a wooden pole, causing fatal cranio-cerebral injuries. Key evidence included the testimony of PW01, an eyewitness who observed the incident, the post-mortem report of Dr. Ratnayake confirming blunt force head injuries as the cause of death, and the investigative findings of PW07 regarding the scene and the weapon. The appellant raised the defence that PW01 fabricated evidence due to business rivalry. On appeal, the appellant argued that the trial judge should have considered a conviction for a lesser offence based on the exception of sudden fight, that PW01’s evidence was not credible, and that the dock statement was not properly evaluated.

The two accused-appellants were indicted in the High Court of Homagama for robbery of Rs.60,000 cash under Section 380 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code (count 1), and the 1st and 2nd appellants were each charged under Section 383 with possessing a deadly weapon, namely a firearm, in the course of the same transaction (counts 2 and 3). The High Court convicted both on count 1, sentencing each to 8 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs.10,000 and a default term of 3 months simple imprisonment; the 2nd appellant was additionally convicted on count 3 and sentenced to 15 years rigorous imprisonment with the same fine and default, and both were ordered to pay Rs.100,000 compensation to PW1. The prosecution case was that on 15 February 2011 three men arrived by car at PW1’s shop, the 2nd appellant brandished a gun, the 1st and 3rd accused went inside and took the money in a tulip bag, and a false number plate fell off revealing the original registration, leading to the vehicle being traced to the 1st appellant. PW1 and PW2 identified the appellants at an identification parade, and police recovered two firearms. The main grounds of appeal urged that the 3rd count under Section 383 offended Section 67 of the Penal Code because the offence formed part of the same robbery, and that the trial judge misdirected on burden of proof and wrongly considered identification evidence. The prosecution conceded the conviction on count 3 was unsafe. The Court of Appeal set aside the 2nd appellant’s conviction and sentence on count 3, affirmed the robbery conviction for both appellants, and, in view of time spent in custody, deducted pre- and post-conviction periods to reduce the 1st appellant’s remaining sentence to 18 months and release the 2nd appellant, while maintaining the fines and compensation.

The Appellant was indicted in the High Court of Colombo under Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance for trafficking and possession of 5.80 grams of heroin on 24 March 2014. The High Court convicted her on the first count (trafficking) and sentenced her to life imprisonment, acquitting her on the second count. The prosecution case was that based on an informant's tip that a woman called 'Nona Akka' and her husband Siril were trafficking heroin near a stairway at Grandpass, a police raiding party waited and apprehended the Appellant and Siril after they alighted from a three-wheeler; the Appellant handed over a parcel from her pocket which tested positive for heroin, and Rs.101,030 in cash was also recovered from her. The raiding party did not include a female officer despite the presence of a female suspect and a nearby police station, they took the suspects to the Police Narcotics Bureau instead of the nearest station causing a delay of over five hours before handing over to the local police, Siril was released without a statement, and the recovered cash was neither recorded in notes nor produced in court. The main grounds of appeal challenged the credibility and probability of the prosecution version, the failure to consider inter se and per se contradictions between PW1 and PW2, and the credibility of the informant, while the Appellant had made a dock statement denying the charge.

The six accused-appellants were indicted in the High Court of Galle on charges of being members of an unlawful assembly with the common object of causing hurt (section 140 of the Penal Code), causing the death of Galla Dehige Gaya Chaminda (section 296 read with section 146), voluntarily causing hurt to Kasthuri Alison (section 315 read with section 146), and alternative charges under section 296 read with section 32 and section 315 read with section 32. The prosecution case was that on 29 January 2011 the 1st and 5th appellants arrived at the deceased's home and the 1st appellant struck the deceased with a belt, and later a group of five or six persons including the appellants returned, dragged the deceased outside and assaulted him with iron rods, causing injuries from which he died on 2 February 2011. The key prosecution witnesses were the deceased's mother-in-law (PW2) and wife (PW3), who purported to identify several appellants, and a police officer (PW6) who confirmed that the deceased's hospital statement did not mention any names of assailants. The High Court convicted all appellants on the 1st, 2nd and 4th counts, sentencing them to six months' simple imprisonment and a fine for the first count and death for the murder counts, while acquitting them on the 3rd and 5th counts. On appeal, the appellants contended that the High Court Judge failed to consider material omissions and contradictions in the testimony of PW2 and PW3, failed to evaluate the fact that the deceased did not name the accused, failed to properly assess the evidence of common object, and did not adequately consider the defence evidence including dock statements. The defence position was that the prosecution evidence was inconsistent and untrustworthy. The Court of Appeal found the evidence of PW2 and PW3 to be wholly devoid of credibility, holding that the prosecution had not proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

The accused-appellant was indicted before the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 9.5 grams of heroin under Section 54(a)(d) and Section 54(a)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance. The High Court convicted her on both counts and sentenced her to life imprisonment. The prosecution case was that on 18 June 1998, acting on an informant’s tip that heroin belonging to a person named Kapila was concealed in a house, excise officers went to the location where the informant pointed out the house and the appellant standing outside; the officers informed the appellant they knew the heroin was there and asked her to hand it over, after which she retrieved from a hole under a pot a cellophane bag containing seven cellophane bags with 644 packets of heroin. The appellant denied the charge and gave a dock statement that she did not know Kapila, that she was taken from her own house to the excise office, and that no heroin was found in her house. The main grounds of appeal included failure to deploy a female officer, the heroin being recovered from neighbouring premises, failure to prove the appellant was the owner of the house, irregularities in the excise inspector’s notes, and failure to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. The defence position was that the appellant had no knowledge of the heroin, was not in exclusive possession of the premises, and was wrongfully arrested.

The five accused-appellants were indicted in the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possession of 152.341 kilograms of heroin (diacetylmorphine) detected on 2 November 2019 aboard the fishing trawler 'Buddhima' in the deep sea, and for conspiracy to traffic heroin. The prosecution led evidence from naval officers PW1 and PW3 who intercepted the trawler, recovered eight bags of suspected heroin from the ice compartment, and maintained custody until handover at port, supported by the Government Analyst's report and documentary records. The High Court convicted all appellants and imposed death sentences. On appeal, the appellants argued that the trial judge failed to consider grave infirmities in the prosecution evidence, misapplied the principle of conscious exclusive possession, erred in finding the chain of custody intact, failed to reject prosecution witnesses for inconsistency and lack of spontaneity, wrongly found conspiracy proved, unjustly shifted the burden of proof, and failed to properly consider the defence evidence. The defence contended that the evidence did not establish actual, exclusive possession or a conspiratorial agreement, that delays in recording statements and non-sealing of productions at sea undermined credibility, and that the dock statements raised reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal dismissed all grounds, holding that the prosecution proved conscious exclusive possession through the confined shared space of the trawler and the collective handling of the contraband, the chain of custody was unbroken, the conspiracy was established by circumstantial evidence, and the trial judge correctly applied the Ellenborough dictum after the defence failed to create doubt.

The petitioner company, St. Anne's Enterprises (Pvt) Ltd, challenged a Customs inquiry decision that imposed a mitigated forfeiture of Rs. 48,327,600.13 and a penalty of Rs. 100,000 on its Shipping Manager for allegedly selling 84,000 kg of RBD coconut oil imported under the Temporary Import for Export Processing Scheme in the local market without paying duties, thereby defrauding customs revenue. The company contended that the inquiry was conducted without due notice to the company, that its employee lacked proper authorization to represent it at the inquiry, that the legal provisions relied upon were defective, and that the inquiry was a sham. Key evidence included the inquiry notes showing the company was not formally notified, the employee representative was himself a suspect, and the inquiring officer referred to written submissions that were never filed. The Customs authorities argued that the employee had implied authority, that the company's partial payment and request for instalments constituted acquiescence, and that a fresh inquiry would serve no purpose given the strong evidence. The Court of Appeal found a violation of natural justice, lack of fair procedure, and that the inquiry was indeed a sham, thereby granting writs of certiorari to quash the orders insofar as they affected the petitioner, and a writ of mandamus directing a fresh inquiry.

This was an application for writs of certiorari, prohibition, and mandamus filed by the petitioner, a dual citizen of Sri Lanka and the USA, seeking to quash a freezing order dated 16 November 2007 issued by the second respondent under the Exchange Control Act and to compel the release of USD 3,000,000 held in a bank account. The funds had been remitted without prior exchange control permission for the purchase of shares. The Central Bank had directed the funds to be frozen pending investigation, and although investigations led to an indictment against third parties that ended in discharge, the freezing order remained in place. The petitioner argued that under section 30(2) of the Foreign Exchange Act, No. 12 of 2017, any pending investigation must be concluded within six months of the Act’s commencement, and that the continued freezing order was unreasonable. The respondents contended that no statutory provision allowed them to lift the directive. The court considered the reasonableness of the order and the interpretation of transitional provisions. No criminal charge or conviction was involved; the petitioner merely sought release of his funds.

The Municipal Commissioner of Galle Municipal Council filed an application in the Magistrate's Court under Section 28A(3) of the Urban Development Authority Law seeking a demolition order for premises No. 166/1, Matara Road, Galle, on the ground that the building was constructed without a valid development permit in a declared development area. The learned Magistrate granted the demolition order, finding that the owner had not obtained a development permit and could not excuse the unauthorised development. The owner invoked the revisionary jurisdiction of the High Court, which dismissed the application, holding that no valid development permit was produced and the Magistrate had considered the relevant issues. The owner appealed to the Court of Appeal, arguing that the Municipal Commissioner lacked legal authority to file the demolition application, that there was no evidence the premises were in a declared development area, and that the proceedings were not instituted in accordance with the Code of Criminal Procedure. The defence maintained that an application for a permit had been submitted and that the construction was not unauthorised, and challenged the Municipal Commissioner's standing to bring the action.

The Appellant was indicted under Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance for trafficking and possession of 4.07 grams of heroin. The High Court of Negombo convicted him on the second count and imposed a sentence of life imprisonment. The case arose from a police checkpoint operation on 6 March 2010 based on information about heroin being transported in three-wheelers; officers stopped a three-wheeler, searched the Appellant who was a passenger, and found a parcel concealed in his underwear. The substance weighed 24.88 grams gross and was found to contain 4.07 grams of pure heroin according to the Government Analyst’s report. The prosecution called police witnesses and the analyst. The Appellant made a statement from the dock. The main ground of appeal was that the trial judge erred in finding the chain of custody proved beyond reasonable doubt, as the Magistrate’s Court released the production to a police constable on 7 June 2010 for delivery to the Government Analyst Department, the analyst’s memorandum was dated 14 June 2010, and the prosecution offered no explanation for the seven-day gap, which cast doubt on the integrity of the exhibits.

This appeal arises from an application under Section 5 of the State Lands (Recovery of Possession) Act No. 7 of 1979 filed by the Deputy Chief Engineer of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority seeking the eviction of the appellant from a state land in Galle. The learned Additional Magistrate of Galle, after inquiry, rejected the appellant's showing of cause and ordered ejectment, finding the appellant to be in unauthorized possession. The appellant's revision application to the High Court of the Southern Province was dismissed, affirming the Magistrate’s order. The appellant appealed to the Court of Appeal, raising grounds that the competent authority’s status was not examined, that the documents marked 1 to 7 demonstrated a government-approved possession, and that the Magistrate failed to provide adequate reasons. The defence contended that the respondent was not a competent authority within the meaning of the Act and that the appellant held a valid written authority, but the Court of Appeal held that under Section 9(1) the only permissible defence was proof of possession under a valid permit or written authority, and none of the produced documents met that requirement. The court further held that the competency of the authority could not be contested at the ejectment inquiry.

The two accused-appellants, who are brothers, were charged in the High Court with the murder of Wijesekara Pathiranage Sarath on 31st October 2004 at Gatamanne, under an indictment containing counts of unlawful assembly and a third count of murder based on common intention. The High Court acquitted them on the first two counts but convicted both on the third count and imposed the death sentence. The prosecution case rested entirely on circumstantial evidence, primarily a dying declaration by the deceased naming 'Thilak' as the shooter, the alleged presence of both accused near the scene shortly after the shooting, and their obstruction of a witness attempting to bring a vehicle to transport the deceased. The wife of the deceased testified to hearing the dying declaration but admitted she could not identify the assailants in the darkness and later named multiple individuals as suspects, creating significant inconsistencies. Evidence showed that several persons in the village were named Thilak, and the crime scene lacked sufficient lighting. The grounds of appeal asserted that the trial judge failed to properly evaluate defence evidence, did not adequately consider the doubt regarding the identification of the first appellant, misapplied the principles governing circumstantial evidence, failed to assess the existence of a common intention between the appellants, and did not consider the possibility of third-party involvement, rendering the judgment inconsistent with the evidence. The defence maintained that the first accused denied the crime and surrendered voluntarily, the second accused claimed to have been elsewhere at the time, and the prosecution had not established beyond reasonable doubt that the 'Thilak' mentioned by the deceased referred to the first accused or that any common intention to commit murder existed.

The accused-appellant was indicted under Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance for trafficking and possession of 11.10 grams of heroin on 27 August 2013. Following trial in the High Court of Colombo, he was convicted on both counts and sentenced to life imprisonment. The prosecution case was that acting on information, police officers arrested the appellant near Sumithrarama temple and recovered a parcel of heroin from his pocket, while the other person with him was later discharged. The principal police witnesses gave contradictory evidence as to the place of arrest, and the officer who originally received the information was not called. The defence position, advanced through a dock statement and supporting witness, was that the appellant was arrested at his residence after the police had arrested another person with heroin and that he was implicated merely because he had telephoned that person. The main grounds of appeal were that the prosecution evidence failed the test of credibility due to material contradictions and a vital missing link, and that the trial judge had reversed the burden of proof and rejected the defence evidence on unreasonable grounds.

The application concerned charges of forging Deed No. 3204 dated 01.07.2007, which affected the proprietary rights of the virtual complainant. The Magistrate's Court acquitted the two accused of those charges. The virtual complainant sought revision in the Provincial High Court, which dismissed the revision application without affording her a hearing. Important evidence before the Magistrate included testimony from Land Registry officials, the Government Examiner of Questioned Documents who highlighted signature discrepancies, and an attesting witness who denied signing the deed. The petitioner contended that the High Court’s summary dismissal violated the rule of audi alteram partem, and that the Magistrate erred in evaluating the evidence, misapplied the burden of proof, and improperly prevented the prosecution from calling the investigating officer. The accused respondents maintained that the Attorney General had refused sanction to appeal, that the revision application raised no questions of law or exceptional circumstances, and that the matter merely involved factual disputes about witness testimony.

The accused-appellant was indicted in the High Court of Kandy on two counts of rape under section 364A(3) and one count of grave sexual abuse under section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code, allegedly committed against his niece, a child under 16 years of age, between 1 January and 6 December 2018. After trial, the High Court convicted him on all three counts and imposed sentences of 20 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 15,000 for each of the two rape counts, 10 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 15,000 for the grave sexual abuse count, and ordered compensation of Rs. 1 million with a default term of two years rigorous imprisonment. The prosecution case was that the accused entered the room where the victim was sleeping, vaginally raped her, and that the victim’s stepmother had witnessed an earlier incident of abuse; medical evidence from the judicial medical officer documented signs of chronic anal penetration and repeated vaginal penetration. The defence contended that the allegations were fabricated due to a land dispute between the accused and the victim’s stepmother. On appeal, the appellant raised multiple grounds, including the prosecution’s failure to call material witnesses, inconsistencies in evidence, lack of credibility of the victim, and deprivation of a fair trial. At the hearing, the State conceded it could not support the convictions on the second and third counts. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal in part, setting aside the convictions and sentences on the second and third counts but affirming the conviction and full sentence on the first count of rape.

The Accused-Appellant was indicted in the High Court of Embilipitiya on one count of criminal trespass and two counts of Grave Sexual Abuse contrary to sections 436 and 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code, committed against a fourteen-year-old minor. The High Court convicted him on all counts and imposed seven years rigorous imprisonment for the first count and fifteen years rigorous imprisonment for each of the second and third counts, with fines and default terms, to run concurrently, and ordered payment of compensation to the victim. The prosecution case was that the Accused, a neighbour, entered the victim's house when she was alone and touched her chest, and on a later occasion at his house caused her to lie down, removed her skirt, and placed his penis on her vagina. The victim testified but was uncertain which incident occurred first, denied parts of her police statement, and her account of disclosing the matter directly to her mother conflicted with her mother's evidence that the mother became suspicious and recorded a conversation before reporting to the police. Medical evidence from the examining doctor revealed old hymen tears and signs compatible with frequent sexual activity and vaginal penetration, whereas the victim described no act of penetration. The grounds of appeal asserted that the trial judge evaluated evidence on surmises, failed to consider inconsistencies and the lack of spontaneity in the victim's evidence, and failed to consider the contradictory medical evidence. The Accused, in his dock statement, claimed he had purchased land from the victim's family, they later demanded he vacate, and the complaint was made after he moved; he denied all allegations of sexual assault.
