The Magistrate's Court acquitted the two accused of those charges. The virtual complainant sought revision in the Provincial High Court, which dismissed the revision application without affording her a hearing. Important evidence before the Magistrate included testimony from Land Registry officials, the Government Examiner of Questioned Documents who highlighted signature discrepancies, and an attesting witness who denied signing the deed. The petitioner contended that the High Court’s summary dismissal violated the rule of audi alteram partem, and that the Magistrate erred in evaluating the evidence, misapplied the burden of proof, and improperly prevented the prosecution from calling the investigating officer. The accused respondents maintained that the Attorney General had refused sanction to appeal, that the revision application raised no questions of law or exceptional circumstances, and that the matter merely involved factual disputes about witness testimony.

The appellant was charged with two counts of murder under section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code for causing the deaths of Willora Arachchige Pemanis Perera and Willora Arachchige Samantha Perera, one count of attempted murder of Ambawalage Siriyawathi under section 300 read with section 32, and one count of mischief to a house under section 419 read with section 32, all arising from an incident on 17 August 1994 at Rambukkana. The High Court convicted the appellant as charged and sentenced him to death on each murder count, ten years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 10,000 and a default sentence of six months rigorous imprisonment on the attempted murder and mischief counts, and ordered Rs. 1,000,000 compensation to PW1 with a default sentence of three years simple imprisonment. The prosecution case centred on the evidence of PW1, the wife and mother of the deceased, who testified that in the early hours while listening to election results she saw the appellant and the first accused near their house, that the appellant attacked her husband with a sword and then attacked her and her daughter, and that the first accused set fire to the house; she identified the accused with the aid of a bottle lamp and a street light. Medical evidence confirmed the husband died from neck injuries, the daughter died from 90% burns leading to septicemia, and PW1 sustained serious injuries. Police officers who arrived shortly after corroborated her immediate complaint naming the appellant and the first accused, and the scene was found with the house destroyed by fire and a pool of blood. The main grounds of appeal challenged the reliability of PW1’s evidence, alleged the trial judge misapplied the Ellenborough and Lucas principles, and argued the appellant’s alibi was not properly considered. The defence position was a denial of involvement and presentation of an alibi that the appellant was helping a politician at another location on the election night.

The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo in case HC/2213/2020 and sentenced on 09/10/2023 for a drug offence involving 3.57 grams of pure diacetylmorphine (heroin). The prosecution case was that acting on information, a police team stopped a lorry at Slave Island, arrested the appellant, and found a substance suspected to be heroin concealed in the knot of his sarong, with a gross weight of about 80 grams. Important evidence included contradictions between the two main police witnesses regarding the distance of the police van from the lorry, the time of return to the police station, the presence of a white paper wrapping, and the use of a friend's van without disclosing his identity. The main grounds of appeal were that the prosecution witnesses failed the test of credibility and probability, and that the learned High Court Judge gave no reasons for rejecting the appellant's dock statement. The defence position was that the appellant was arrested while he had come to Slave Island to load a mattress into the lorry and that no drug offence had been committed.

The appellant was indicted before the High Court of Ratnapura along with another for abetment and conspiracy to commit the murder of Rajapakshalage Gamini Rajapakshalage alias Shantha and for committing that murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code. The High Court acquitted the co-accused but convicted the appellant on the count of murder and sentenced him to death. The prosecution case was that the deceased's wife, the co-accused, had an illicit affair with the appellant and had eloped with him about a month before the incident; the deceased was found stabbed to death at his residence. There were no eyewitnesses, and the case rested solely on circumstantial evidence. Key evidence included the testimony of a 16-year-old witness who claimed to have seen the appellant running from the direction of the deceased's house at night, identifying him from behind with torchlight, and the recovery of a knife under Section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance that was not conclusively linked to the murder. The defence denied involvement, and the appellant appealed on grounds that the circumstantial evidence was insufficient, the identification was unreliable, the trial judge erroneously shifted the burden of proof, and the Section 27 recovery was not properly evaluated.

The accused-appellant was indicted in the High Court of Ratnapura for the murder of Kankanamlage Punchi Banda alias Nilame under section 296 of the Penal Code and for causing simple hurt to Mahakandawatta Arachchilage Manjula under section 315. The High Court convicted him on the murder count and sentenced him to death. The prosecution case, supported by eyewitnesses PW1 (the appellant's brother) and PW2, was that the appellant suddenly attacked PW2 and the deceased with a knife at the appellant's residence where his bedridden father lay. The Judicial Medical Officer recorded twenty injuries on the deceased, nineteen of which were sharp-cutting wounds, and three grievous injuries; cause of death was shock and hemorrhage. The appellant made a dock statement claiming he attacked because PW2 had struck his father's head against the wall. On appeal, the appellant contended that he acted under grave and sudden provocation and should have been convicted under Exception 1 to section 294 (culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297) rather than murder. The main grounds of appeal were that the High Court failed to properly analyze the evidence favourable to the defence, wrongly rejected the defence evidence, and that the prosecution did not prove murder beyond reasonable doubt.

The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession of heroin for sale. On 22 February 2002, acting on information, a police raiding party arrested the appellant in front of a house and recovered from his sarong a cellophane bag containing 195 small packets; the substance tested positive for heroin, and the gross weight after removing the bag was 7 grams. The prosecution relied on the evidence of the raiding officer, other police witnesses, and the government analyst. The defence maintained that the informant’s information was not recorded, the premises identified in the information were not searched, a weight discrepancy existed between the 7 grams recorded by police and the 7.44 grams noted by the analyst, and the trial judge refused to permit the appellant to call a defence witness, violating the right to a fair trial. The appeal was advanced on the grounds that the trial judge failed to evaluate the evidence properly and that the production chain was not established beyond reasonable doubt.

The accused-appellant was indicted in the High Court of Anuradhapura on seven charges arising from a road traffic accident that occurred on or about October 19, 2008 at Mihintale, where the bus he was driving caused the death of four individuals and hurt to three others. Charges 1 to 4 were for causing death by a road traffic accident not amounting to culpable homicide punishable under section 298 of the Penal Code, and charges 5 to 7 were for causing hurt endangering life or personal safety by a road traffic accident punishable under section 328 of the Penal Code. At the conclusion of the trial, the learned High Court Judge convicted the appellant on all charges and sentenced him to a fine of Rs. 1000 with 3 months simple imprisonment in default and a substantial term of 5 years rigorous imprisonment on each of the first four charges, fines of Rs. 100 on the fifth, sixth, and seventh charges, and ordered payment of Rs. 100,000 as compensation to the next of kin of each deceased and Rs. 25,000 to each injured person. The appellant appealed against the conviction and sentence but at the hearing disputed only the sentencing order. The defence submitted that the appellant was 63 years old, a first-time offender suffering from health issues that would make incarceration challenging, expressed remorse, and proposed to pay an additional Rs. 1,000,000 each to the next of kin of the four deceased. The prosecution argued that motor traffic accidents resulting from driver negligence have reached epidemic proportions and that the court must consider the seriousness of the offence and the need for deterrence. The main ground of appeal was that a non-custodial sentence should be imposed given the appellant's age, health, remorse, and the seventeen years that had elapsed since the offence.

The accused was indicted before the High Court of Galle for possession and trafficking of 382.3 grams of heroin under Section 54A(d) and (b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance. Following trial, the High Court convicted him on both counts and imposed the death sentence. The prosecution case was that on 15 May 2001, acting on an informant’s tip, police officers arrested the accused outside a house in Galle carrying a black shopping bag containing a nickel-coloured iron box with drugs, a scale, and weights; the substance was later confirmed by the Government Analyst to be 382.3 grams of pure heroin. The accused in his defence stated he was renting a room in the house owned by one Susil Kumarasiri, was arrested while asleep, and was falsely implicated in order to secure the release of Kumarasiri, who had also been arrested but later set free. The main grounds of appeal were the suspicious role of the informant, time and distance discrepancies, absence of independent evidence, the weight of the defence case, and the release of Susil Kumarasiri. The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution had proved the accused’s exclusive possession of the heroin, the proper custody and sealing of the production, and that the arrest and release of another person did not raise a reasonable doubt, and accordingly dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction and sentence.

The 1st Appellant, a police officer, was charged with soliciting and accepting a bribe of Rs.10,000 and Rs.5,000 from the complainant to prevent the prosecution of a suspect for possession of elk meat, and the 2nd Appellant was charged with abetting those offences and directly accepting a bribe, under Sections 16(b), 19(c) and 25(2) of the Bribery Act. The High Court of Colombo convicted both Appellants on all counts and sentenced the 1st Appellant to four consecutive terms of 7 years rigorous imprisonment with fines, and the 2nd Appellant to four consecutive terms of 7 years rigorous imprisonment with fines. The case arose from a police raid on the complainant’s hotel where the Appellants seized suspected elk meat, arrested an employee, and allegedly solicited a bribe to protect the employee from prosecution; a trap was later organised and the 1st Appellant was arrested after accepting money. The prosecution relied on the complainant, his son, and Bribery Commission officers, but material contradictions emerged as to whether the seized meat was elk or beef and whether the suspect was actually prosecuted in the Magistrate’s Court. The essential witness Leelasena, the suspect, was not called by the prosecution. The Appellants’ main grounds of appeal were that the charge was unsustainable given the suspect had been produced in court, the complainant was an unreliable witness, the omission to call Leelasena caused prejudice, and the contradictions destroyed the credibility of the prosecution case. The defence maintained that the Appellants had lawfully arrested the suspect and performed their duties, and that the bribery allegations were fabricated out of a prior grievance.

The Accused-Appellant was indicted in the High Court of Colombo under Section 3(1) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act for depositing Rs.13,968,802.66, being proceeds of heroin trafficking, into a Sampath Bank savings account. Upon pleading guilty, she was convicted and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment, the statutory minimum. The appellant, a mother of two, claimed she acted on her husband's instructions and was unable to pay a fine. The sole ground of appeal was that the sentence was excessive; the defence argued that minimum mandatory sentences are unconstitutional and that courts retain judicial discretion to impose a non-custodial sentence, relying on Supreme Court Reference 03/2008 and related decisions. The Court of Appeal rejected this argument, distinguishing the reference as applicable only to a different statute, and held that the minimum sentence under the Money Laundering Act must be imposed, affirming the conviction and sentence.

The accused-appellant was indicted in the High Court of Badulla for the murder of W. M. Lalani Renuka on or about 14 May 2002, an offence under section 294 of the Penal Code. Following his plea of not guilty, he absconded and was tried in absentia; the High Court convicted him of murder and sentenced him to death on 9 March 2012. The prosecution relied on eyewitness testimony, particularly that of PW1 and PW9, and medical evidence that the stab injuries inflicted were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, with no evidence of sudden and grave provocation, mistake, or accident. The appellant filed a petition of appeal only on 23 September 2021, nearly nine years after the conviction, making it grossly out of time. On appeal he sought to invoke the revisionary jurisdiction of the Court of Appeal, arguing that procedural technicalities should not override a fair evaluation of his case and that exceptional circumstances existed to prevent a miscarriage of justice. He offered no valid explanation for his prolonged absence or the delay, and the State objected that the appeal was time-barred and that the appellant’s contumacious conduct disentitled him to relief.

The appellant was charged in the High Court with two counts of murder under section 296 of the Penal Code and one count of attempted murder under section 300, arising from an incident on 23 March 2008 after a police station settlement regarding maintenance, in which he led his wife and mother-in-law to a precipice near a temple, allegedly pushed them down and stoned them, causing the mother-in-law's death, the death of his child (whose body was later recovered), and injuries to his wife. The High Court convicted him of the second count (murder of the child) and the third count (attempted murder of the wife) and imposed a death sentence for the murder and 15 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine and compensation for the attempted murder. Key prosecution evidence included the testimony of the injured wife, medical findings that the child died from manual strangulation and facial injuries and that the wife sustained life-endangering injuries, and the discovery of the child’s body following information given by the appellant while in custody under section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance. The main grounds of appeal challenged the credibility of the wife’s testimony due to inconsistencies, the proper application of section 27 recovery, the evaluation of the defence case, and alleged denial of a fair trial from excessive judicial questioning and irregular corrections to the record. The appellant’s defence was that a verbal altercation led to an accidental grappling fall down the precipice, after which the wife threw stones at him, denying any intention to kill or cause injury.

The applicant invoked the revisionary jurisdiction of the Court of Appeal seeking to set aside an order of the Provincial High Court of Hambantota dated 18.07.2025 in case HCRA 21/2025. The High Court had exercised its concurrent revisionary jurisdiction to set aside an order of the Magistrate’s Court of Hambantota in case 2425/25 and directed the Magistrate to hold an inquiry under Chapter VII of the Primary Courts Procedure Act. The respondent raised a jurisdictional objection that the Court of Appeal cannot sit in revision over an order made by the High Court in the exercise of its parallel revisionary jurisdiction, as both courts enjoy coordinate jurisdiction and the applicant had exhausted the remedy. The Court of Appeal upheld the objection and dismissed the application in limine with costs.

The petitioner, a metal quarry operator, filed a writ application under Article 140 of the Constitution seeking certiorari to quash a certificate dated 19.08.2020 issued by the first respondent (Assistant Commissioner of Labour) under section 38(2) of the Employees' Provident Fund Act, and mandamus to direct a fair inquiry. The certificate alleged the petitioner employed the third to eleventh respondents at a land called Wanapoluhena and failed to pay EPF contributions from January 2013 to November 2018. The petitioner denied employing these persons, stating he had only one employee, and contended that no inquiry was held and he was not afforded a hearing before the certificate was issued, violating natural justice. Evidence included a labour officer's report (1R1) that inconsistently identified K.W. Premadasa as both the employer's representative and an employee, and notices sent to multiple addresses without confirmation of receipt. The respondents argued the petitioner was guilty of laches and had suppressed facts. The main grounds of appeal were breach of audi alteram partem and failure to ascertain the correct employer before initiating proceedings.

The accused-respondent was indicted in the High Court of Colombo on twenty-two counts: one count of cheating under section 403 of the Penal Code and twenty-one counts under section 25(1) of the Debt Recovery (Special Provisions) Act No. 02 of 1990 as amended, arising from a series of dishonoured cheques and counter-orders made between March 2015 and October 2016, involving amounts including an alleged defrauded sum of Rs. 7,945,000. Before trial, the accused raised a preliminary objection that the Debt Recovery Act conferred exclusive jurisdiction on the Magistrate's Court for the offences in counts two to twenty-two, and that the Attorney General could not include them in a High Court indictment. The High Court accepted this objection and directed that only the first count proceed. The Attorney General appealed, arguing in the main grounds of appeal that the High Court judge erred in holding that the offences could not be tried in the High Court and in failing to give effect to section 393(7) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, which empowers the Attorney General to forward an indictment directly to the High Court for any summary offence, thereby removing the Magistrate's jurisdiction.

The appellant was convicted in the High Court of Ampara of kidnapping a minor girl from lawful guardianship under section 354 of the Penal Code and grave sexual abuse by placing his penis on the girl’s vagina under section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code, and sentenced to 7 years rigorous imprisonment on the second charge. The prosecution alleged that after bathing at a tank, while the group collected kon fruits, the victim moved to collect firewood, and the appellant dragged her into the forest and committed the sexual act. The victim (PW01) testified that she was held from behind, lost consciousness, and was unaware of any criminal activity, providing no direct evidence of sexual abuse or identification of the appellant. Two eyewitnesses, PW03 and PW06, claimed to have seen the appellant and victim in a compromising position but gave contradictory accounts regarding their state of undress. The defence contended that the appellant had gone home after bathing with the group and did not participate in any such acts. The main grounds of appeal were that the trial judge failed to consider inherent weaknesses and contradictions in the prosecution case, acted on hearsay evidence, and imposed an excessive sentence. The Court of Appeal found that the High Court judge had improperly reviewed and relied on the contents of the victim’s prior statement recorded in the Police Information Book as substantive evidence, which is impermissible in law, and on that basis interfered with the conviction.

The petitioner, the 17th accused, was indicted with others on charges including murder and attempted murder, later amended to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297 read with section 32 of the Penal Code and other offences. He pleaded guilty in the High Court to counts 1 to 10 and count 20. The incident occurred between pro-ragging and anti-ragging groups at the University of Jayawardenapura, where the deceased sustained 37 injuries, and eyewitnesses identified the petitioner as having assaulted the deceased with a club. The High Court judge found the petitioner to be the principal offender with greater criminal liability and sentenced him on count 2 to eight years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 5,000, along with lesser concurrent sentences on other counts. The petitioner sought revision on the ground that the sentencing judge failed to consider mitigating circumstances and that the sentence on the second count was excessive.

The appellant appealed to the Court of Appeal against the order of the High Court of Ratnapura dated 02.05.2019, which in its revisionary jurisdiction affirmed the Primary Court’s order dated 22.08.2017 in a land possession dispute under the Primary Courts Procedure Act. The respondent filed information alleging that she and her deceased husband had peacefully cultivated the land since 1981 and that the appellant, having no claim, was attempting to forcibly dispossess her, creating a threat of breach of the peace. The appellant failed to appear on the returnable date despite substituted service and was deemed in default; the Primary Court conducted the inquiry in his absence. The appellant later filed a motion with an affidavit explaining non-receipt of summons and requesting an opportunity to participate, but the Primary Court did not address this application. The High Court, in revision, held that the default was properly entered and that the Primary Court correctly ignored the unsupported application. The main grounds of appeal were that the High Court erred in law by not finding the Primary Court’s failure to consider the application to purge default and the appellant’s filed affidavit as material under section 66(8)(b) to be an error. The defence position was that the appellant had not been served with summons and that his affidavit asserting his claim should have been taken into account by the Primary Court. No criminal offence, conviction, or sentence was involved; the proceedings concerned solely the determination of possession under preventive jurisdiction.

In High Court of Colombo case HC/3748/2007, the accused respondents were convicted and sentenced on 5 May 2022. The aggrieved party filed a revision application on 14 October 2022 seeking to set aside the sentencing order and requesting the Court of Appeal to impose appropriate sentences in view of the aggravating circumstances of the case. The revision was dismissed in limine solely on the ground of unreasonable and unexplained delay without any consideration of the merits.

The petitioners, operating under the business name G.T.A. Service Station, filed a writ application seeking mandates in the nature of certiorari, prohibition, and mandamus to quash an award dated 11.09.2020, a subsequent notice dated 11.03.2022, and a certificate issued by the Commissioner of Labour under Section 8(1) of the Payment of Gratuity Act directing payment of gratuity totaling Rs. 420,940.00 to three employees. The petitioners contended that the employees were not employed by G.T.A. Service Station because the dates of first employment predated the commencement of that business, and that the real employer was a different entity, General Trade Agency. The 1st and 2nd respondents objected, raising issues of unexplained delay of nearly three years and the existence of an alternate remedy before the Magistrate's Court where the certificate had been filed and the petitioners had already shown cause. The court, without considering the merits of the employment relationship, dismissed the application on the grounds that the petitioners were guilty of laches and had an equally effective alternate remedy available under the proceedings instituted in the Magistrate's Court.

The defendant-petitioner filed an application for restitutio in integrum and revision challenging an order of the District Court of Mount Lavinia in case No. 1195/23 RE that had been affirmed by the Civil Appellate High Court of Mount Lavinia. The plaintiff-respondent raised preliminary objections that the petitioner should have sought special leave to appeal from the Supreme Court and could not avail multiple remedies. The Court of Appeal, following the Supreme Court's decision in SC/Appeal/65/2025, held it had no jurisdiction to review a judgment or order of a Provincial High Court exercising appellate jurisdiction, whether by way of appeal, revision, or restitutio in integrum, as such jurisdiction is vested exclusively in the Supreme Court. The application was dismissed with no order for costs.

The accused-appellants, along with two others, were indicted before the High Court of Colombo on 14 counts of soliciting and accepting a bribe from Nishshanka Arachchige Sumathipala between 1 May 2012 and 8 August 2012, punishable under sections 16(b), 19(c) read with section 25(2) of the Bribery Act. The first accused-appellant was convicted on counts 1, 2, 9, and 10 and sentenced to a total of twelve years rigorous imprisonment and fines; the second accused-appellant was convicted on counts 3, 4, 11, and 12 and sentenced to a total of ten years rigorous imprisonment and fines, with compensation ordered. The prosecution arose after the complainant, engaged in sand mining without a valid permit, alleged that four wildlife officers solicited a bribe to avoid legal action. The complainant initially testified that all four officers asked for money and that the fourth accused demanded Rs. 30,000; after the trial judge released him on a personal bond and adjourned the case, the witness later claimed he was under threat and altered his testimony, a contradiction the trial judge did not address. The main grounds of appeal were that the trial judge improperly questioned the witness, assumed the role of an advocate, released the witness on bond without evidential basis, and thereby deprived the accused of a fair trial. The accused-appellants made dock statements and maintained that the judge's intervention vitiated the proceedings.

The appellant was indicted in the High Court of Galle for murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code and robbery under Section 380 of the Penal Code, allegedly committed on May 11, 2005, when the deceased caretaker was found dead in a ransacked house and Rs. 128,400 worth of property stolen. The High Court convicted the appellant on both counts, sentencing him to death for murder and 10 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine for robbery. The prosecution case was that the appellant sold a stolen jewelry item (marked ε03) to PW05 the day after the incident, and relied on the presumption of recent unexplained possession of stolen property under section 114 of the Evidence Ordinance. PW05 testified he purchased the jewelry from the appellant between 11:00 and 12:00 on May 12, 2005, but investigating officers gave contradictory evidence about the time of recovery, with records showing the appellant’s arrest at 19:05 and first visit to PW05 at 23:05 that night. The main grounds of appeal challenged the sufficiency of circumstantial evidence, admissibility of certain evidence, and rejection of the dock statement. The appellant’s defence was that two individuals approached him to assist in selling jewelry to help a sister travel abroad, for which he received Rs. 2,000, and he had no involvement in the murder or robbery.

The appellant was indicted in the High Court of Matara on two counts of procuring a person to become a prostitute contrary to section 360A(1) of the Penal Code. The High Court convicted him on the first count (procuring Kidalampitiyage Deepthi Chandrika) and acquitted him on the second, sentencing him to seven years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 25,000, and compensation of Rs. 100,000 to the victim. The prosecution case was that PW01 and PW02, while returning from an alms-giving, agreed to go to a hotel in Matara Fort managed by the appellant to engage in sexual activity with two men for payment; the appellant offered them a meal, informed them of the men's arrival, and introduced PW01 to a man who turned out to be a raiding party officer and arrested them. The appellant’s defence was that PW02 had previously visited the hotel, she contacted him before coming, he served lunch, and when two men sought a room without valid identification he refused, whereupon they revealed themselves as police and arrested him. On appeal, the appellant contended that the testimonies of PW01, PW02 and PW03 were contradictory, the trial judge failed to consider legal principles on decoy evidence, the appellant’s evidence raised reasonable doubt, and the sentence was excessive. The Court of Appeal found that PW01 and PW02 had voluntarily decided to engage in prostitution and that the appellant did not procure their involvement, relying on the interpretation that section 360A(1) does not apply to persons already willing to engage in prostitution.

The appellant was indicted for possession and trafficking of 2.24 grams of heroin under Section 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance. The High Court of Chilaw convicted him and imposed a sentence of life imprisonment. The prosecution case was that, following a raid based on information and the arrest of three other suspects, the appellant was apprehended after a decoy telephone call and a small parcel of heroin was recovered from the hem of his undergarment. Important prosecution evidence included the testimonies of two raiding officers (PW1 and PW2) and an Assistant Government Analyst (PW12). The defence maintained that the chain of custody of the alleged heroin was not proved, highlighted material contradictions between PW1 and PW2 regarding the number of officers, vehicles used, the place and manner of the search, and the description of the undergarment, and noted the absence of contemporaneous notes on sealing, odometer readings, and the identity of the officer to whom the production was handed at the Government Analyst's Department. The main grounds of appeal were the failure to prove the chain of productions, the lack of credibility of PW1 and PW2, inadequate reasons for rejecting the dock statement, and the excessiveness of the sentence.

The accused was charged before the High Court of Matara with attempt to murder under Section 300 of the Penal Code for an incident on 11 November 2012, where he allegedly attacked his brother (Prosecution Witness No. 1) with a knife over a dispute concerning inherited paddy land. The prosecution evidence, including testimony from the victim and a Judicial Medical Officer, established that the victim sustained 18 injuries, some serious and life-threatening, while the accused also had non-grievous injuries and a physical disability in his left hand. The defence claimed that the victim attacked first with a knife and the accused retaliated in self-defence; this version was not put to the victim in cross-examination. The High Court convicted the accused and imposed a sentence of 8 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 1000, and compensation of Rs. 200,000. The appeal was brought on grounds that the trial judge misdirected himself in law and fact, failed to properly analyse the evidence and the defence case, did not consider the absence of recovered weapons, and failed to adequately assess the elements of the offence and the accused’s identity. The appellate court held that the conviction was sound but found the sentence excessive and lacking reasons, and substituted a suspended term of 2 years rigorous imprisonment and reduced the compensation to Rs. 150,000.

The matter arose from an information filed under section 66(1)(b) of the Primary Courts' Procedure Act alleging a land dispute likely to cause a breach of the peace between the Petitioner-Petitioner-Respondent and the Respondents-Respondents-Appellants regarding a land at Godella, Ratnapura. The Magistrate acting as Primary Court Judge held the Appellants entitled to possession. On revision, the Provincial High Court set aside that order and held the Petitioner-Petitioner-Respondent entitled to possession. The Petitioner-Petitioner-Respondent relied on a 2016 annual license, tax payments for 2017 and 2018, and a fertilizer subsidy letter from a tea association to establish longstanding possession, and alleged the Appellants entered and cut trees. The Appellants claimed possession for over fifty years through their predecessor, contending the permit was irregularly issued and suspended, and that the Respondent was merely connected by marriage. The main grounds of appeal were that the High Court order was contrary to law, failed to adhere to the mandatory procedural framework under the Primary Courts' Procedure Act, incorrectly evaluated evidence, and failed to consider whether the Magistrate lacked jurisdiction due to police proceedings under section 81 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The accused-appellant was indicted for the murder of a 7-year-old child. Following a trial by jury in the High Court, he was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The appellant, a soldier, had taken in the deceased, his wife's nephew, to provide shelter and education. On the day of the incident, while teaching the deceased mathematics, the appellant inflicted corporal punishment on the child for failing to memorise numbers. The deceased was later taken to hospital and pronounced dead. Key prosecution evidence included testimony from a 14-year-old household member who heard the appellant hitting the child and the deceased pleading not to be hit, and the Judicial Medical Officer's evidence that injuries were compatible with blunt trauma and a fall, were not necessarily fatal but could be fatal in the ordinary course of nature, and caused death by shock and haemorrhage from multiple contusions without fractures. The appellant admitted using corporal punishment for discipline but claimed the deceased fell down the stairs. The main grounds of appeal were that the trial judge misdirected the jury by failing to explain the legal principles of murderous intention and the distinction between murder and culpable homicide not amounting to murder, and that the evidence supported a conviction only for the lesser offence. The defence position, conceded by the prosecution, was that the appellant lacked murderous intention and that the incident occurred under grave and sudden provocation, warranting substitution of the murder conviction with culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

The second and fourth accused appellants were indicted in the High Court of Chilaw for murder, allegedly committed on or about July 27, 2010, at Pothuwatawana by causing the death of the deceased. After trial, the High Court convicted them and sentenced them to death. The prosecution case was that the deceased, accompanied by PW01, visited a boutique where the fourth accused appellant was present; the fourth accused contacted the third accused, who arrived and together they argued with the deceased and pushed him to the ground; then the first accused and the second accused appellant arrived, the first accused slapped the deceased, and the second accused appellant and the third accused assaulted the deceased with sharp-edged weapons, causing injuries from which the deceased died. The post-mortem report (P1) gave the cause of death as bilateral hemothorax and multiple stab injuries to the abdomen. The appellants denied involvement and relied on pleas of alibi. The main grounds of appeal were that the prosecution had failed to prove the appellants’ presence at the scene beyond reasonable doubt, and that the learned High Court Judge misdirected herself on the legal principles applicable to the defence of alibi by not evaluating the alibi holistically against the entirety of the prosecution evidence and by not reaching a finding that the identity of the appellants at the scene had been established beyond reasonable doubt.

The case originated from a report by the Officer-in-Charge, Mahiyangana Police, in Magistrates Court case B 26134 regarding an investigation into the robbery of vehicle bearing registration number UP PH 7874. The report included a witness statement. The learned Magistrate directed the absolute owner, Arpico Finance Pvt Limited, to produce the vehicle to court. The registered owner, Abeydora Arachchilage Chandani, obtained interim release of the vehicle on a bond, but upon objection by the absolute owner, the Magistrate on 01.10.2019 ordered the vehicle returned to court custody pending an inquiry and directed written submissions. The registered owner filed a revision application in the Provincial High Court of Badulla seeking to set aside the Magistrate's order and stay the return directive; the High Court dismissed the application on 24.08.2023. The registered owner appealed to the Court of Appeal, challenging the High Court's dismissal and maintaining that the Magistrate's order was wrong. The absolute owner contended the appeal was frivolous.

The appellant was indicted for the murder of his wife under Section 296 of the Penal Code. The High Court of Badulla convicted him and imposed a death sentence. The case involved the appellant striking his wife on the leg with an iron pipe during a heated argument, allegedly provoked by an extra-marital affair, while he was under the influence of liquor. The deceased developed toxaemia from soft tissue damage and died three days later. Key evidence included the testimony of the son, the deceased’s dying declaration, the judicial medical officer’s post-mortem findings, and the weapon. The appellant’s defence was that he lacked murderous intention, having acted in the heat of passion without premeditation, and that the evidence established only knowledge of likely death, warranting a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 297. The main ground of appeal was that the trial judge failed to appreciate the absence of mens rea and misapplied the third limb of Section 294, given the nature of the injury and the circumstances of provocation.

The Accused-Appellant was indicted in the High Court of Vavuniya on four counts: robbery of gold jewellery from Kanthiah Muttiah and Muttiah Parameshwari using a deadly weapon, punishable under Section 383 of the Penal Code read with Section 32, and the murder of both individuals, punishable under Section 296 read with Section 32, all arising from the same transaction on or about 19 January 2012. The High Court convicted the Accused-Appellant on all counts and imposed sentences of ten years rigorous imprisonment for each robbery count and the death penalty for each murder count. The case was based entirely on circumstantial evidence. The deceased couple resided on their agricultural land, and the Accused had worked for them approximately one month prior to the incident. The female deceased was found with her fingers severed and jewellery removed. The prosecution relied principally on evidence that the Accused made a telephone call to the male deceased on the day of the incident summoning him, and on the recovery of the deceased's jewellery, mobile phones, and an axe pursuant to a statement made by the Accused under Section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance. The Accused-Appellant appealed on grounds that the trial judge misapplied the principles governing Section 27 recoveries, erred by shifting the burden of proof, and that the circumstantial evidence was inadequate and improperly evaluated. The defence position, given in a dock statement, was a complete denial of involvement, asserting that the Accused was fishing when arrested, was assaulted by police, made no confession, and that no recoveries were made at his instance.

The Accused-Appellant was indicted in the High Court of Monaragala for murder under section 296 of the Penal Code for causing the death of Herath Mudiyanselage Samantha on or about February 8, 2018. The prosecution case was that at a party a dispute led to the appellant slapping the deceased and that later the deceased was found with a fatal cranio-cerebral injury to the left scalp. The High Court convicted the appellant and sentenced him to death. The appellant denied inflicting the fatal injury. The sole ground of appeal was that the trial judge failed to properly appreciate the identification evidence. Key prosecution witness PW11, who saw the deceased walking past followed by another person, could not identify that person as the appellant, and another witness PW02 saw only the earlier slapping. The Judicial Medical Officer opined the scalp injury could have been caused by a fall. A stained wooden pole was recovered based on the appellant’s statement but no analysis linked it to the deceased or the injury. The defence maintained that the unidentified individual could not be excluded as the perpetrator and that there was no evidence placing the appellant at the scene when the fatal injury occurred.

The appellants were charged in the High Court with murder under Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code and with simple hurt under Section 314 read with Section 32. The High Court convicted them of murder and sentenced them to death. The prosecution case was that on a Poya Day when the deceased and his companions were returning from a temple, a verbal exchange and exchange of blows occurred between the deceased and the second appellant, after which the first appellant stabbed the deceased once in the chest; the deceased died from haemorrhagic shock due to a single stab injury. The key prosecution evidence included the Section 33 deposition of a witness who had died before completing his testimony, in which he stated that the second appellant struck the deceased and the first appellant stabbed him, and the evidence of another witness who saw the deceased fall but did not see the stabbing and identified the first appellant by moonlight. The first appellant denied the charge in a dock statement, and the second appellant gave sworn evidence raising an alibi that he was on duty as a watcher at a library, calling two supporting witnesses. The main grounds of appeal asserted that the trial judge failed to adequately evaluate the credibility of the sole identifying witness, failed to consider material contradictions, failed to properly consider the second appellant's alibi, and failed to consider whether the evidence attracted the exception of a sudden fight under Exception 4 to Section 294 of the Penal Code.

The Accused-Appellant was indicted before the High Court of Puttalam for possession and trafficking of 20.41g of heroin under Section 54 of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, convicted on both counts, and sentenced to life imprisonment. The prosecution case was that on 29 October 2013, police officers on roadblock duty at Lunulinda Junction searched a three-wheeler in which the Accused was a passenger and found a yellow parcel marked 'W50' containing heroin in his right shorts pocket, with a net weight of 49.857 grams and a pure heroin content of 25.41 grams. The Accused gave evidence that the police planted the drugs. On appeal, the grounds urged included that the trial judge failed to consider the prosecution's failure to prove the chain of custody of the productions to the Government Analyst beyond reasonable doubt, failed to give conscious consideration to contradictions and inherent improbabilities in the prosecution story, and failed to properly consider the Accused’s dock statement. Important evidence highlighted was an inconsistency in the testimony regarding the handling of productions on 30 October 2013: PW01 stated he received the production from PW11 at 9:30 a.m., while PW11 testified he received the productions only after they were weighed at the hospital at around 11:40 a.m., and PW04 claimed he handed the production to PW01 for measurement, creating significant doubt about the integrity of the inward journey.

The accused-appellant was charged under Section 296 of the Penal Code with the murder of Rajakaruna Mudiyanselage Chaminda Bandara alias Gamini on 30 November 2005. After a non-jury trial, the High Court of Gampaha convicted him of murder and sentenced him to death on 15 November 2021. The prosecution evidence showed that the deceased was a factory worker renting a house with a cousin, PW10, who awoke at night to find the appellant standing beside the deceased holding a knife; the appellant fled. PW9 testified that the appellant, who was on duty that night, appeared distressed and disclosed that his wife was having an illicit affair with the deceased. The JMO recorded six cut injuries to the neck and opined that death resulted from neck bleeding caused by a sharp cutting weapon. The sole ground of appeal was that the trial judge failed to adequately consider the mitigatory plea of cumulative provocation, which the defence argued should have reduced the conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 297 of the Penal Code based on Exception 1 to Section 294.

The appellant, the registered owner of a vehicle, appealed against the confiscation of his vehicle ordered by the Magistrate’s Court and affirmed by the High Court. The vehicle had been used by the appellant’s driver to transport teak and burutha timber without a permit, an offence under section 26 read with section 40 of the Forest Ordinance, and the driver was convicted upon his plea of guilty. In the subsequent confiscation inquiry, the appellant, as a third-party owner, sought to avoid confiscation under the proviso to section 40(1), claiming he had taken all precautions to prevent the unlawful use of the vehicle. His evidence was that he had permitted the driver to use the vehicle solely to transport building materials for the driver’s house, had instructed the driver not to use the vehicle for any illegal activity, warned that any such misuse would result in termination of employment, and obtained a letter from the Grama Niladhari confirming the construction. The main grounds of appeal were that the lower courts had misdirected themselves on the law regarding the proviso and failed to properly evaluate the evidence. The Court of Appeal held that the precautions taken were superficial, consisting of mere instructions without a thorough assessment of risks or additional deterrent measures, and dismissed the appeal.

The accused-appellant was indicted in the High Court of Vavuniya under sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance for possession and trafficking of 1,135 grams of heroin on 9 November 2017. After trial, the High Court convicted him on both counts and sentenced him to death on each count. The prosecution case was that a police team led by PW1, acting on information, arrested the appellant at the Vavuniya old bus stand and recovered a parcel of heroin from a NIKE bag in his possession; the parcel was initially weighed at the police welfare shop as 2.266 kilograms. The Government Analyst’s report later recorded a heroin weight of 1,982 grams. The main grounds of appeal were that no proper raid was conducted, the prosecution story was improbable due to material inter se and per se contradictions in the evidence of PW1 and PW2 concerning where and when the information was received and the sequence of events, and that the chain of custody of the production was not proved beyond reasonable doubt, particularly given the significant weight discrepancy. The defence took the position that the prosecution evidence was unreliable and failed to establish the case beyond reasonable doubt; the appellant gave a dock statement and did not call other evidence.

The accused-appellant was charged in the High Court of Kandy with murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code for causing the death of Muthuthanthrilage Alex Udaya Perera on or about February 16, 2010. Following trial, the High Court convicted him and imposed the death sentence. The prosecution case was that the appellant, the son-in-law of the deceased, visited the deceased's home where his wife had been staying after a matrimonial separation; after she refused to return with him, a quarrel ensued, the deceased intervened, and the appellant left briefly before re-entering and fatally stabbing the deceased in the kitchen. The stabbing was witnessed by the appellant's wife (PW01) and another daughter of the deceased (PW02). The Judicial Medical Officer determined the cause of death as internal hemorrhage from a stab wound, with the injuries being necessarily fatal. The appellant denied involvement and maintained his innocence. The sole ground of appeal was that the trial judge failed to consider the contradictions and omissions in the evidence of PW01 and the contradictions between the evidence of PW01 and PW02.

The accused was indicted for rape punishable under Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code, but the High Court convicted him of grave sexual abuse under Section 365(b)(2)(b) and sentenced him to 12 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 20,000 with a default sentence of 6 months simple imprisonment, and compensation of Rs. 200,000 with a default sentence of 1 year simple imprisonment. The prosecution case was that the accused committed the offence on Kachcakaduwage Champika Fernando; evidence was led from 8 witnesses and productions P1 to P3 were marked, and the accused made a dock statement. The expert judicial medical officer confirmed there was no penile penetration, and the prosecutrix's testimony was found to be inconsistent and lacking credibility. The main grounds of appeal included that the trial judge erred by convicting on an unaltered indictment, failed to comply with criminal procedure, and denied the accused an opportunity to defend the charge of grave sexual abuse; the accused's defence was directed solely at the rape charge. The Court of Appeal set aside the conviction and sentence, finding that the accused had been gravely prejudiced and the conviction was unsafe.

The appellant, the registered owner of a tractor and trailer, appealed against the judgment of the High Court of Matara which had dismissed his revision application and affirmed a Magistrate’s order confiscating the vehicles under Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance. The confiscation followed the conviction of several accused for unlawfully transporting ten jackfruit logs. The owner testified that he had known the driver for 8–10 years, had given the vehicle only for nearby hires, kept it at his home, retained the keys, and had no knowledge of the offence. The main grounds of appeal were that the lower courts misdirected themselves by failing to consider the owner’s uncontradicted evidence that he had taken all precautions to prevent the use of the vehicle for the offence, thereby satisfying the required proof on a balance of probabilities. The defence position was that the offence was committed without the owner’s knowledge and that all necessary preventive measures had been taken.

The appellants were charged in the High Court of Kurunegala with conspiracy to commit murder and murder of Rathnayake Mudiyanselage Anusha Hemanthi Rathnamali Rathnayake under sections 296, 113B, 102, and 32 of the Penal Code for an incident on or about September 19, 2005. The High Court convicted them on both charges and sentenced them to death. The prosecution case was that the deceased, a fuel station clerk, accompanied the manager to a bank to deposit collections, stated she would visit a relative, did not return, and her body was found the following day near the fuel station; evidence included testimony from the manager, the deceased’s father and sibling, and the discovery of the body. The accused consistently denied any involvement in the incident. On appeal, they contended that they were deprived of a fair trial because the trial judge failed to call upon them for the defence as required by section 200(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act after the close of the prosecution case, and because newly assigned counsel for the first appellant was forced to proceed without adequate preparation time when the trial resumed on the same day. The Court of Appeal set aside the conviction and sentence and ordered a retrial.

The accused-appellant was indicted for the murder of Jagodage Indika Rangajeeva on 18 June 2010 under Section 296 of the Penal Code. After a non-jury trial, the High Court of Embilipitiya convicted him and sentenced him to death on 20 November 2024. The prosecution case was that PW11, who had been sexually abused by the deceased, sought the appellant’s help; she called the deceased to the appellant’s house where, after drinking tea, both felt faint and the deceased was found dead. Medical evidence showed death from neck pressure and gagging, with injuries from manual strangulation and a blunt weapon. The dead body, an axe, and a motor bike were recovered upon the appellant’s statement under Section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance. PW11, originally committed, was later made a prosecution witness. The appellant’s defence was that he was not at home at the time of the incident and that PW11 had summoned him after the fact. The main grounds of appeal were that the High Court judge erroneously concluded the appellant and PW11 committed the murder without evidence, wrongly admitted recovery evidence under Section 27 because the location of the body was already known to the police, and unreasonably rejected the defence. The appeal also challenged the reliance on PW11 as an unreliable accomplice and highlighted material contradictions in her evidence.

The petitioners, the Principal and Manager of Sri Devarakshitha Pirivena, sought writs of certiorari and mandamus in the Court of Appeal challenging the decision of the Pirivena Education Board to revoke the registration of the pirivena, as communicated by letter dated 27.02.2024. The pirivena had been registered since 2006, and its registration was cancelled following inspections revealing unsatisfactory conditions, including low student attendance, administrative irregularities, and allegations of misconduct by the first petitioner. The petitioners argued that the decision was tainted by mala fides and that they were not afforded a fair hearing. The Court found that the respondents had complied with the procedure set out in Regulation 10 of the Pirivena Education Regulations, the petitioners had been given an opportunity to show cause and had responded, and no evidence of malice was established. The court held that the decision to cancel registration was not ultra vires, unreasonable, or in breach of natural justice, and dismissed the application, declining to issue formal notice.

The Accused-Appellant was convicted by the High Court of Hambantota for the murder of T.B. Jeewani Samanmallee, a 12-year-old girl, under Section 296 of the Penal Code and sentenced to death. The deceased was found stabbed in her home; the case rested on circumstantial evidence. The Appellant, her brother-in-law, had been staying at the house while the mother and stepfather were away. A neighbour saw the Appellant leaving hastily around 9.30 a.m. carrying a bag. The body was discovered later that day. The prosecution relied on last-seen evidence, recovery of the deceased's school bag and a knife sheath at the Appellant's arrest, and a knife and trousers recovered from a culvert based on a statement under Section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance; DNA on the knife and trousers matched the deceased. The main grounds of appeal included that the circumstantial evidence was insufficient, the time of death was not established, the involvement of a third party (the stepfather) was not excluded, material contradictions existed in identification of the bag and clothing, and the trial was unfair due to the exclusion of defence photographs and improper use of police statements. The defence maintained innocence, contending that the evidence did not irresistibly point to guilt and that investigation failures and alternative inferences rendered the conviction unsafe.

The petitioner, a Chief Petty Officer in the Sri Lanka Navy, was charged under Section 104(1) of the Navy Act with possessing 180 milligrammes of cannabis, alleged to have been found in a small piece of paper that fell from his bag during a search at the entrance to the Navy Camp in Trincomalee in June 2020. Following a Summary Trial, the Presiding Officer found him guilty and recommended dismissal from the Navy without disgrace. The prosecution relied on evidence from the sentry and another sailor who was present; the petitioner made an unsworn written statement denying possession and suggesting the substance may have been introduced. The petitioner challenged the conviction and sentence by way of writ, principally on the grounds that the Presiding Officer failed to give reasons for the finding as required by Sri Lanka Navy Order 0501 item 06(n) and improperly considered the preliminary investigation report rather than confining the decision to the evidence led at the trial, in violation of natural justice and prescribed procedure.
